analysis.one_liner: Blocks big local phone company mergers unless regulators find they boost competition.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a Senate committee or floor vote; it died in the Judiciary Committee with no cosponsors after Senator Leahy introduced it in May 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Clayton Act to stop any large local telephone company (one serving more than 5 percent of the nation's phone access lines) from merging with or buying another large local phone company unless the Attorney General finds the merger would promote competition and the Federal Communications Commission finds the companies have fully carried out the 1996 Telecom Act's interconnection rules — the rules that let competitors plug into the local phone network [S2][S3]. If either regulator finds otherwise, courts could block the merger [S2][S3]. The Attorney General would also have to report merger analyses to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Telephone customers and telecom competitors. Local phone markets in 1999 were dominated by a handful of large regional companies, and this bill would make further consolidation among them legally much harder unless regulators certified it would promote competition and that the companies had opened their networks to rivals as required by the 1996 Telecommunications Act [S2][S3]. That protects rivals trying to compete for local service, and preserves the competitive pressure that keeps local phone rates and service in check [S2].

how_it_helps.text: A large local phone company (over 5% of U.S. access lines) could not merge with or acquire control of another unless the Attorney General found the deal would promote competition for local exchange and access services [S2][S3].

The merger could also not go forward unless the FCC found each company had fully implemented the Communications Act sections 251 and 252 interconnection requirements — the rules requiring the Bell companies to open their networks to competitors — for at least half the access lines in each state served, half of them residential [S2][S3].
Federal courts could block mergers inconsistent with either finding, and the Attorney General could sue in any district where a defendant resides, is found, or has an agent [S2][S3].

The Attorney General would have to submit an analysis of each merger's competitive effects to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees within 10 days of finding the deal promotes competition, creating public accountability for merger approvals [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large local telephone companies and their affiliates. They would face a new, stricter pre-merger approval gate: deals among big local carriers could be stopped even when they might otherwise pass standard antitrust review, and the companies would have to file applications with both the Justice Department and the FCC simultaneously [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Large local phone companies seeking mergers

drawbacks.text: Prior-approval requirements add delay and cost to merger reviews, and some mergers between large carriers could produce real efficiencies; the bill would condition all such deals on regulator findings, potentially blocking consolidations that standard antitrust law would allow [S3].

The FCC compliance condition covers only half of a company's access lines in each state (half of those residential), so a company could satisfy the test while leaving competition short of full implementation on the rest of its network [S2][S3].
The bill preserves all existing antitrust and FCC authorities rather than replacing them, meaning merging companies would face overlapping reviews by two agencies and the courts [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted response to a wave of consolidation among regional Bell companies. The benefit is stronger protection for local phone competition, which historically translates into lower prices and better service for households. The cost is slower, more duplicative merger review for large carriers, and a compliance test that is only partial (half of access lines). On balance it favors consumers, though it adds regulatory friction and its coverage threshold is imperfect.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 1999 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it; it died at the end of the 106th Congress without a vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Senator Leahy introduced the bill on May 25, 1999, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
No other senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
The bill received no further action after referral — no committee markup, no floor vote — and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large regional telephone companies were better off because the bill died: they faced no new pre-merger gate, and the era of big local-carrier consolidation (such as SBC-Ameritech, completed in late 1999) could proceed under ordinary antitrust review rather than the bill's stricter competition and interconnection tests.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large regional phone companies wanting to consolidate

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; no other senator joined him

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (106th Congress)
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill out; it died in committee at the end of the 106th Congress

sides.party_line_note: There were no cosponsors and no votes, so the partisan shape of support and opposition never showed up in the record; the only recorded action was referral to a Republican-controlled committee.

industries.industry: Large local telephone companies (regional Bell carriers over 5% of U.S. access lines)
industries.note: The bill would bar mergers among them unless regulators found the deal promotes competition and the companies had opened their networks to rivals. They profit from consolidation and had resisted full compliance with the 1996 Act's interconnection duties, so their interest ran against the public's interest in competitive local service.

industries.industry: Competitive local exchange carriers and telecom rivals
industries.note: The bill would preserve the competitors' ability to interconnect with the big local networks, which is the basis of their ability to compete for customers. Their fortunes rise and fall with the public's interest in phone competition.
